📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Fitbit Air is one of my favorite products of 2026 and my preferred workout companion, but not being able to see a workout while you’re in the middle of it has been a huge complaint of mine, and the latest Google Health patch is fixing that.

Quite literally at the start of this week, I was on a walk through my neighborhood and though to myself, “it’s still pretty annoying that I can’t see my workout progress in the Google Health app.” It’s been a complaint of mine for a while, as various treadmill sessions and more have left me wondering what my heart rate is looking like, how many steps I’ve taken, etc, and it’s only a problem when using the Fitbit Air, seeing as the Pixel Watch (or Fitbit Edge) I’d wear otherwise will show that data front and center.

Google Health 5.13 is fixing that.

According to recent reports, in the changelog for Google Health 5.13, Google details a new “exercise in-progress” card on the main “Today” screen. This will show what exercise is being tracked and also let you end the workout early.

Recent findings suggest that if you use your Pixel Watch, Fitbit Air, or Fitbit Edge to automatically track your exercises, you’ll now see an exercise-in-progress card on your mobile app’s Today screen. This card lets you know that your device is tracking your exercise and gives you the opportunity to end the tracking and get your summary whenever you want.

We don’t know exactly what this card looks like just yet, but it sounds like it fits the need perfectly.

Google Health 5.13 is now rolling out on Android and iOS.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that after noticing that his Elecbrakes remote had automatically paired to a stranger's trailer, Patrick Forck's cybersecurity spider senses tingled.
  • Recent findings suggest that the story goes that Forck was a contented user of the Elecbrakes solution for the trailer towing fraternity.
  • In a recent development, forck and McCarthy's first step on the road to a solution was to use Claude to do the heavy lifting on the reverse engineering of the Elecbrakes Android app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after noticing that his Elecbrakes remote had automatically paired to a stranger's trailer, Patrick Forck's cybersecurity spider senses tingled. Any feelings of foreboding were warranted, as it was discovered that a critical Bluetooth security flaw meant anyone could connect to an Elecbrakes controller "without pairing, authentication, a PIN, or any approval." Over the following 10 months, Forck and his Element Digital colleague Jeremy McCarthy would fully identify the vulnerabilities, make responsible disclosures to the vendor, work on fix verification, and more.

Recent findings suggest that the story goes that Forck was a contented user of the Elecbrakes solution for the trailer towing fraternity. The firm's systems are claimed to be easy DIY plug-and-play controllers for enhanced braking response – notable for trailer towing, especially with larger and heavier loads. The core functionality wasn't a problem, but Forck was alarmed when driving down the highway one day and noticed that his Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else’s trailer. "It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea," explained our tech-savvy protagonist. It wasn't long before he thought, "If a device I don’t own will happily talk to my in-car remote driving past with zero friction… what exactly is stopping my phone or any other Bluetooth device from talking back?" Clearly, Elecbrakes ' ease of use was unintentionally too powerful.

In a recent development, forck and McCarthy's first step on the road to a solution was to use Claude to do the heavy lifting on the reverse engineering of the Elecbrakes Android app. McCarthy built a Web Bluetooth research tool that runs in Chrome, again using Claude. Then Forck tested the newly built tool with his car and trailer on some gravel roads on his family estate. It was confirmed that any attacker could connect via Bluetooth from nearby without Bluetooth pairing or authentication. Moreover, they could send simple commands to the trailer, apply braking at any force level, and receive confirmation that the brake had engaged.

As per the blog post documenting the finding and fixing of these vulnerabilities, the danger of a security flaw which "outputs torque to a wheel on a public road," is difficult to overstate. Especially when the attack surface and opportunity are open to “anyone within Bluetooth range.”.

With the bulk of research complete, the Element Digital colleagues disclosed the information to Elecbrakes in May 2026. They were pleased with the small firm's responsiveness and openness. By July, firmware updates to patch the EB2 and VM1 models currently on the market were released.

An older Elecbrakes controller called the ELBC 2000 was discovered to have the same Bluetooth security flaws. The vulnerability of this model, which hasn't been sold for a number of years, has now been confirmed by the maker. Nevertheless, some folks will be using it on public roads. Elecbrakes has advised owners to keep an eye on firmware update notices for an impending fix.

#92828. Breaking: MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

Breaking: MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes.
  • Industry observers note that until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a newly introduced approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

Industry observers note that until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

It has been revealed that researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a newly introduced approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

"We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," notes Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

Industry observers note that chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller.

Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

Sources indicate that the team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

Industry observers note that the physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

Sources indicate that to solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

In a recent development, "The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates new capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How states.

Teaching a Tiny Robot to Proposal Difficult Maneuvers.

The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

Sources indicate that although this method requires substantial computing power, it can proposal difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

Repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each new flip under the proper conditions.

Industry observers note that "If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How says.

The researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate rapidly enough for real-time flight.

A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

"The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

Sources indicate that experiments highlighted that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

"This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up newly introduced opportunities for multimodal locomotion," notes Hsiao.

In a recent development, the team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a newly introduced position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

"This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen claims.

Toward Autonomous Flying Microrobots.

One major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

The team also prepares to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

"For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a upcoming control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," notes Chen.

This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

"It stayed alive for so long" - Behind the wheel with the Last Riders saying goodbye to GTA Online, amidst GTA 6's world-changing launch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the decade or so since Grand Theft Auto Online's arrival, its roads have become a kind of home; well-loved by its racers, its gear heads, and speed freaks.
  • Sources indicate that so when the GTA Online community decided to host Last Ride events this week - a sort of mass in-game road trip and a communal farewell before attention inevitably turned to GTA 6 - I was keen to join in.
  • Sources indicate that kirsty is one of the many long-time players who chose to embark on their own last drive as part of the event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the decade or so since Grand Theft Auto Online's arrival, its roads have become a kind of home; well-loved by its racers, its gear heads, and speed freaks. It's a game that allows players to lose themselves in the roleplay, the heists, and the crime sprees. But for me, an occasional dipper into its major updates, the car folk have always been the engine driving its appeal.

Sources indicate that so when the GTA Online community decided to host Last Ride events this week - a sort of mass in-game road trip and a communal farewell before attention inevitably turned to GTA 6 - I was keen to join in. The Last Drive was scheduled to begin an hour before GTA 6's launch, and would see numerous groups embarking on their own journey across GTA Online's servers, all taking the same route: starting at Los Santos' Del Perro Pier and following the highway around Los Santos' entire perimeter before finally rolling up to its airport. Players would then fly off into the sunset, close the game, and move on. Some just for a while, others perhaps forever.

Sources indicate that kirsty is one of the many long-time players who chose to embark on their own last drive as part of the event. She runs the Fast Crew racing community in GTA Online and has been playing since the beginning in 2013, even meeting her fiance through the game. Unlike some, however, she plans to stick around in GTA Online after GTA 6's release, at least until the latest game's equivalent comes along.

It's the social dynamic of GTA Online that makes it special, Kirsty tells me when we speak online, and she calls it a community of players "that thrives from supporting each other, racing together and just having fun". She points to GTA Online's 30-player sessions as one reason for its enduring appeal "That's important for people in communities like ours," she explains. "Gaming is an escape to many people, a distraction or a coping method. GTA is special because it stayed alive for so long, giving people that escape.".

Then there's Brittany, who leads the GTA Online Ascent racing community. Brittany has a real-life kart racing background, and built race tracks across various Xbox 360 games before arriving in GTA Online. As with many of the players I spoke with, the in-game connections Brittany made have blossomed into real-life friendships, all built around racing.

Industry observers note that "GTA Online introduced me to many lifelong friends," they explain. "Hell, I even met my girlfriend Ari through the GTA Racing community. Every year, five-to-six of us go to the Indy 500 and all of us met through my [GTA Online] PC racing community BRITCAR." Brittany was also planning their own Last Drive, using old cars from the game's earlier years.

Sources indicate that it's clear GTA Online has become more than just a game to many people, and I was eager to see how players might choose to say goodbye. So as GTA 6 loomed, I booted up GTA Online and prepared for my own Last Drive, waiting near the pier in a random online lobby. Slowly, other people started to arrive - all seemingly strangers - and at the allotted time, we slowly began making our way around the map as one.

Recent findings suggest that what I saw was brilliant. A snaking line of customised cars, custom paint jobs, and underlighting, slowly navigating the island; a peaceful, reverential convoy of players who weren't blasting away at each other with weapons for once. The chaos of the typical GTA Online lobby never broke out. Instead, there was a sort of unspoken armistice between those eager to enjoy one last moment in a game they'd spent so much time in. Gradually, more people joined our conga line.

Industry observers note that besides being a lovely way to close a chapter for many, it allowed for a cheeky bit of peacocking too. Many players pulled up in truly exceptional rides: there were supercars, bulky muscle cars, and street-racer lightshows, all as much an expression of their owners' personalities and tastes as any human avatar.

Recent findings suggest that at one point, the leader of this snaking pack made a wrong turn, taking us into a dockyard and an unfortunate dead-end. We then all had to slowly reverse out - a time-consuming, if amusing, process which allowed one opportunistic spectator to pull up and take a few of us out with a well-placed RPG. But after we'd all reconvened nearby, the respectful atmosphere resumed. No flying Oppressor Mk II rained missiles on us, and there weren't any kamikaze crashes interrupting our final drive.

When we did finally reach the airport, people left their vehicles and things took a more knockabout turn. Together we huddled for a few moments, letting off gunfire and fireworks into the night. Then the cops came, and the group rushed to steal planes and helicopters before things got wilder still.

In a recent development, slowly, eventually our group began to disperse. Players either went on to cause some final havoc before GTA 6's arrival, or they did as I did, flying over the ocean into the sunset before leaving the server once and for all. It sounds sappy but it was moving. Here, a game perhaps best known for its player-versus-player hijinks had - thanks to a close-knit community consisting of people like Kirsty, Brittany, and all their friends - became a wholesome drive along. A send off to the game as it was, before ushering in a new dawn.

It speaks to what is special about GTA Online, really. A playground people have spent years in, clearly still important to them, and a chance to say a farewell of sorts from the place they feel most comfortable: behind the wheel.

It has been revealed that A short clip can help a project in different ways. It can show an idea you have not filmed, put an existing design in motion, or give an announcement something to look at. The same approach will not work if the clip needs to demonstrate a real feature or show exactly what happened. Before choosing a generator, decide what the viewer needs to learn from the shot.

Industry observers note that this article uses Kling 4.0 as a worked example, but the decision process applies to any AI video generator. It covers how these tools turn prompts and images into video, how Kling 4.0 and a few alternatives differ, how to choose a starting mode, how to add exact text and branding outside the generated clip with a short ffmpeg script, and when real footage is the better choice. Feature details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing and change often, so confirm current terms before you initiative a production.

● Generated video is best for imagined shots. It suits concepts, backgrounds and early explorations, not instructions or faithful records.

● Your starting material decides the mode. A written idea, a reference image or a pair of opening and closing frames each call for a different input.

● Keep exact wording out of the generated clip. Titles, dates and logos belong on separate layers in an editor.

● Tools differ on control, cost and licensing. Compare inputs, length, resolution, credits and terms before you commit.

● Always review. Watch the whole clip at its final size and check it against the real product or design.

In a recent development, most current systems extend diffusion models across time. A model learns to turn noise into a coherent set of frames guided by a prompt, and sometimes by an image or a clip. The research paper Video Diffusion Models describes this extension from images to video. The practical consequences are easy to observe.

● The prompt describes change over time. One visible change and one camera instruction usually work better than a long list of actions.

● Reference material steers but does not lock. A picture can suggest shape and colour without guaranteeing an exact match.

● Longer clips give more room for drift. Faces, logos and fine text are the first things to change between frames.

● Cost grows with length and resolution. Most hosted tools charge credits per second, so short previews are cheaper than full shots.

If you only have an idea, start with text. For a short announcement, you might ask for a band of light to move across a wall of coloured tiles. No one needs to recognise a particular wall, so the model can decide how it looks. Give it one visible change and a clear view of the subject. A prompt such as Soft morning light travels slowly across a wall of blue ceramic tiles. Fixed camera, no lettering is enough to see whether the idea works.

It has been revealed that if you already have an illustration or a photo, reference mode gives you another starting point. Suppose you want a short concept clip for a desk accessory that only exists as a drawing. The picture can show the general shape and colour while the prompt describes the view you want. A video reference can help when it is the motion that is hard to explain, such as a slow camera slide. Say what each asset is meant to guide, and do not add a clip just because you have one.

Recent findings suggest that use keyframes when a particular view matters at a particular moment. Start with an opening image. If a short reveal also needs to end with the object facing forward, add an ending image to show that view. That is different from a reference image that mainly indicates what the object looks like. Neither method guarantees an exact match, so check the result rather than assuming the uploaded picture has locked the design.

No single tool fits every project. The table summarizes what each option’s own page states, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

Reading the table: hosted studios such as the one on JXP are the quickest way to test an idea and need no setup, but you pay per second and work within their supported inputs. Kling’s own site is the place to check announcements and API options directly, since its page says little about durations or resolution. Runway positions its models for motion quality and prompt following, while Google’s Gemini API video documentation suits teams building generation into their own products. The Diffusers video guide covers open-source pipelines for developers who want local control and are ready to manage GPUs and licences.

Trying an idea before making it. An illustrator might want to see how an imagined landscape feels when the light changes. A quick clip gives the team something to discuss: is the change visible, and does it happen at the right pace? It does not need to be the final animation to answer those questions.

Showing a product concept. A rotating view or a slow camera move can help people discuss how a design might be presented. It is useful early, when the shape and lighting are still being explored. Once the clip represents a product someone can buy, the standard changes. If a port moves or a button appears that the real product does not have, it is the wrong clip for that job.

Making a short visual for a post. A few seconds of moving colour can give an event announcement or a project update a distinctive opening. Put the name, date and other exact wording in your editor so they are readable and easy to change. The background only needs to support the message. If it competes with the text, use less movement or keep the background still.

Generated video is unreliable at lettering, so add titles in an editor or with a script. The command below overlays a title on a generated background and then checks the file properties. It assumes you already have a clip named background.mp4 and ffmpeg installed.

-vf "drawtext=text='Launch Night | 12 March':fontcolor=white:fontsize=64:x=(w-text_w)/2:y=(h-text_h)/2:box=1:boxcolor=black@0.35:boxborderw=24" \.

-c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -an announcement.mp4.

ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 \.

-show_entries stream=width,height,r_frame_rate,duration \.

-of default=noprint_wrappers=1 announcement.mp4.

Because the text lives in the command, you can reuse the same background for three events by changing one string. The font may need to be set with a fontfile option on some systems. This is the practical version of keeping the moving background in one file and the editable details in another.

According to recent reports, if people will follow the clip as instructions, use real footage or a screen recording for the steps. A convincing shot of an app is not proof that a button is in the right place. A generated close-up of a product is not a reliable way to show how its parts fit. You can still use an imagined opening, but make the switch to the real demonstration clear.

In a recent development, think about revisions, too. If your team expects to adjust the same title, logo or date every week, put those elements on separate layers in an editor. And if the only movement you need is a slow zoom on an approved picture, apply that zoom directly. There is no reason to risk changing the picture when a simple edit will do.

This matters when someone else will maintain the video. A reusable announcement template is easier to hand over if the moving background is one file and the event details are editable. If the team likes the movement but needs three versions with different dates, they can reuse the same clip. If every change calls for a latest generation, the time you saved on the first version may disappear on the second.

The Kling 4.0 video generator on JXP presently offers 720p and 1080p settings and clip lengths from 3 to 30 seconds. According to its page, reference mode accepts up to 10 images and 5 videos, keyframe mode takes a first frame, middle frames and an optional last frame, and credits are charged per second with a higher rate at 1080p. For a first attempt, choose the frame shape you blueprint to use and make the clip only as long as it needs to be. Check the displayed credit cost before generating, because a short preview can tell you whether the direction works before you spend on a longer shot.

It has been revealed that decide what a good result looks like before you generate it. For the tile background, you need to see the light move without distracting from the words you will add. For a product concept, check whether the shape stays recognisable as the viewpoint changes. Watch the whole clip at the size the audience will see it. If the shot misses the point, revise one thing at a time: the motion, the framing or the source image.

#92824. Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software.
  • Sources indicate that scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons.
  • "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," noted Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the newly introduced study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a newly introduced way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

Sources indicate that scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

"We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," noted Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the newly introduced study published in Nature.

A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction.

The strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

In a recent development, quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

Recent findings suggest that to fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The newly introduced results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

It has been revealed that "Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," said Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes.".

Why Non-Abelian Anyons Are Different.

According to recent reports, ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

In a recent development, these anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a upcoming type of particle with its own unusual rules.

"The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen said.

Each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

Because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

Why Braiding Alone Was Not Enough.

In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

That experiment demonstrated that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

"In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," said Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough.".

Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations.

For the upcoming study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

It has been revealed that the S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

According to recent reports, the underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

In a recent development, by combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

"It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," said Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers.

The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

The experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

"So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen mentioned.

According to recent reports, the next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on new techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Where to start with Queen's Domain? It's tempting to begin with King's Field; after all, FromSoftware's seminal first-person action-RPG is an explicit inspiration for developer Freshly Baked Games. But 40 hours later, it feels like so much more. It's equally tempting to invoke another FromSoftware game: Dark Souls. Queen's Domain owes an obvious debt to that game's celebrated level design: the dazzling interconnectedness of its vertiginous world. But that's not quite right either. The deeper you delve, the more there's something of the spirit of The Legend of Zelda, a touch of Metroidvania too. Until finally you concede that Queen's Domain, with its remarkable world of densely packed secrets, is very much its own.

Industry observers note that all this begins with an island. You, Prince Beruim, are a castaway, washed ashore on Neasied. Your father, the king, has disappeared, and your search has brought you, somewhat circuitously, here. As you clamber to your feet and survey the island, it makes an immediately striking impression: all strange peaks and crooked spires; a cramped, chaotic mass of landmarks lost amid the dense undergrowth. Pyramids perch atop steep plateaus; a vast, moss-tinged mausoleum sprawls across the land to one side while the other is dominated by an imposing tower. It's a world made all the stranger by Queen's Domain's retro aesthetic. Here, shimmering low-res textures and low-poly shapes converge to create elaborate spaces and structures that feel slightly at odds with the lo-fi vibe. It's not quite old, not quite latest; instead, something of a world lost outside of time. It makes for an enigmatic, disorientating landscape. And when paired with a soundtrack that delights in discordance, as it swings from gentle ambience to pulsing synths, it's a mood that refuses to resolve.

There is so much to say about Neasied. And so much I absolutely will not spoil. But very early impressions don't do it justice at all. As you take your first tentative steps onto the island, presented with a forking path that eventually winds back in on itself, it's easy to mistake Queen's Domain for a first-person Dark Souls - especially if, like me, you're only passingly familiar with King's Field. As in most Soulslikes, early progress is defined by a punishing inch-by-inch crawl from one brutal encounter to the next; where death - via chicken-cricket hybrids, ladybird-rats, and other wonderfully odd things - comes fast and frequently, respawning you back at the last Crystal Monument you visited. And because its wilfully old-school design eschews modern-day niceties such as a combat lock-on or dedicated roll button, there's a looseness to fighting that takes a while to click. But it does, slowly, click.

This is a game that demands you lean into its limitations, encourages you to find ways to make them work. At first, those Souls-honed instincts are likely to be your undoing as you naturally scramble for a dodge button that isn't there. But soon a different sort of pattern emerges: you realise that to avoid a ladybird attack, you simply need to step back - but not so far you don't have time to nip in and strike while your opponent takes a pause. A charging enemy might require a different approach - a well-timed backstep and swivelling sideways strafe to put you in the right place for a counter. And in this way, combat becomes a compelling sort of puzzle as you learn each of the 100+ enemies' little ticks - including rock, paper, scissors-style weaknesses to different weapon types - and figure out how to respond.

There's more to consider. Your melee damage output, for instance, is directly tied to your stamina bar: the more stamina you have, the harder you'll hit; too low and it's a waste of a swing. That forces you to choose your moments carefully, moving out to safety while your bar refills. And there's a charge attack, also linked to your stamina, that does more damage still. Already combat has a distinctively deliberate rhythm, but then come your first throwing knives. These are most immediately useful against enemies ordinarily out of reach - like the laser-spewing foliage dogging your journey early on - but they're equally valuable for luring individual enemies away from the throng. Throwing weapons take a while to return to your pouch, meaning they too need to be deployed with purpose. And while knives are just the start - you'll acquire an increasingly exotic selection of throwables including poison-tipped darts and homing blades - they all fundamentally work the same way.

And the interplay of these various warm-ups and cooldowns creates an increasingly engaging rhythm as you learn to juggle between your variously equipped weapons to maximise their damage potential. You might, for instance, fire off a one-two-three volley of homing darts, then use a magic lantern to toss out a massive fireball that bounces destructively around the room. And it's there, in the ensuing chaos, you'll charge up your blade, letting rip then returning to your darts again. Combat might encourage a methodical pace, but that doesn't mean you can't fight fast, and there are some fascinating synergies among the various weapons, many having their own wonderfully distinct mechanisms. There's a brawling gauntlet that lifts you clean off the ground and a vampiric blade capable of stealing an enemy's life force. There are hammers, creatures, and an unexpected mid-game weapon class, utilising a third rechargeable power source, that I am definitely not spoiling. Queen's Domain's 100 or so weapons create ample space for experimentation and customisation, and the further from its cautious beginnings you stray, the brisker, the more exhilarating its combat becomes. In my current, late-game form, I'm a whirl of blades and blasts and up-close attacks that feels anything but Soulslike.

Queen's Domain isn't just a nippier sort of game, though. It swiftly reveals itself to be friendlier, more accommodating. Levelling, for instance, happens passively as you play, meaning every swing feels like it's contributing to your progress. Weapons level independently too, encouraging specialisation. There are no flasks, no accumulated currency you'll need to worry about dropping on death, no subsequent corpse runs. And progress can be saved at any time using the nearest Crystal Monument, meaning that when you respawn, you won't have to grind through the same opponents again. Enemies do eventually reappear of their own accord, so you can't exploit the save system indefinitely. But unlike Souls-style bonfires, Crystal Monuments only repopulate the world when you explicitly tell them to - when you Rest to clear status effects and restore health - giving you considerably more agency. You can decide when to push forward, when to retreat and lock in your progress, and when to reap the benefits of a rest and reset. Together, it makes for a breezier, less punishing, more consistently rewarding riff on the traditional Souslike, while never losing that I-can-do-this just-one-more-turn allure.

It has been revealed that but as immensely enjoyable as Queen's Domain's combat is, the real draw here, unquestionably, is the world. Neasied is extraordinary. Right from the start, as you pick yourself off the sand and survey the landscape, its enigmatic huddle of peculiar landmarks isn't just intriguing, it's inviting. These odd pyramids, these curious plateaus practically demand to be explored. But how? The answer comes perhaps an hour in when, fancily clad skeleton boss successfully slain, you get your hands on the Holy Sword Endu. It's an immediate boon, far more lethal than the rubbish rusty blade you've been wielding so far. And its secondary attack - a long-range jab that propels you forward - is handy too. It's also your key to unlocking Neasied.

Endu's violent forward momentum can, you see, fling you across previously uncrossable gaps, gradually carrying you further and further as more upgrades reveal themselves. Suddenly, Queen's Domain takes flight, quite literally, becoming something closer to an exploratory sandbox as it adopts the spirited acrobatics of a platform game. And as you experiment with your newfound freedom, the more paths you explore, the island begins to take on a dizzying latest form. Neasied, when viewed from up high, reveals itself to be a vastly intricate traversal puzzle. That peculiar structure in the distance? If you can find an appropriate ledge to fling yourself from, it's now yours for the investigating - and from there, one, two, three more tantalising branches are revealed. Neasied is an astonishing piece of design: a ludicrous, elaborate tangle of hidden pathways and secrets, forever folding in and around itself, that's crafted to invite curiosity and then constantly reward.

In a recent development, freshly Baked Games always feels one step ahead. I can't recall a single moment where my exploratory What-ifs - What if I throw myself this way? What if I do a falling mid-air turn? What if I toss myself down this hole? - didn't bear fruit. Sometimes your prize is a steaming platter of boon-granting food, sometimes it's another bit of increasingly exotic weaponry. Perhaps you'll find a strange NPC with a favour to ask; fish eggs and mysterious skulls; a shopkeeper with a thing for ducks (who, in a typically lovely touch, festoons his store with the goods you're willing to sell), and so many mysterious upcoming puzzle threads to pull. As you fling and probe and push on forward, that thing you've been carrying around for hours - or, conversely, that thing you saw hours ago - suddenly finds new purpose. There's a definite touch of Metroidvania as old areas reveal new truths the further you go. And because there's so little handholding, so little explicit direction, every discovery feels like your own.

But just as you think you're starting to get a handle on Queen's Domain's shape, along comes another surprise: dungeons as vastly intricate as the world outside. You'll navigate labyrinthine waterlogged caverns of angry fish where progress involves puzzling past ancient mechanisms. Later, an arcane tower where gargoyles prowl. Here, the convoluted upward route takes circuitous laps among the endless bookshelves, spilling out the windows onto teetering precipices with alarming sea views. Then down, however briefly, to eerie chambers below. Suddenly, the mood is less Soulslike, more Zelda, and your expectations shift again. And still upcoming discoveries lead to new paths and fresh mysteries.

And it keeps on going. As Freshly Baked Games gradually peels back Neasied's layers, it constantly finds new ways to awe: yet more surprises, yet more secrets, your exploratory digressions earning still more intriguing rewards. There comes a point where you think surely you must have seen everything, explored its deepest caverns and most mysterious tombs, but down you go again. And somewhere around the midpoint, Queen's Domain takes a truly audacious turn. There is a - let's call it a tonal lurch for fear of spoilers - that signals another shift. Suddenly, there are new toys to play with, an autumnal landscape so complex in its demands, it genuinely made my brain pulse. And then it's over. Until it's not.

There are, it turns out, secrets beneath the secrets; a still more intricate web of interconnected threads spun throughout this already fascinating, impossibly complex world. The Neasied that welcomes you really is just the tip of it all. Exactly when you'll come to this realisation depends how thorough you are in the earlier hours - how willing you are to explore its darker corners and brave its more punishing realms - but for me the before-and-after managed to divide my 40-ish hour playthrough neatly in two. You reawaken with a sense of a quest unfulfilled, a hint that more is required. And so, in lieu of more explicit direction, you set out again, probe deeper, explore further, and slowly the vaguest shape of a new objective - a succession of tiny threads seemingly all leading in the same direction - begins to emerge. Tucked along uncharted paths, perhaps, or in suspicious corners, or in item descriptions that suddenly feels like clues.

Sources indicate that it's here in this second half - something of a dark mirror to the first, in classic Zelda style - that Queen's Domain takes on a more esoteric air; its web of distantly scattered enigmas requiring real dedication to unfurl. Why this pot on a stick? Why this book? How do these unlit lanterns relate to this thing, and that thing, and this other thing on the other side of the world?

Recent findings suggest that it's clever stuff, even if navigating its late-game threads can occasionally feel just a little too much, a little too abstruse, and you'll potentially face a lot of needle-in-a-haystack backtracking if you haven't been taking judicious notes as you go. Do I have any other quibbles? There are perhaps too few boss encounters that feel like genuine events. And while combat generally feels fair and balanced, serving as a propulsive drumbeat to the broader exploratory rhythms, there are a few late-game all-the-enemies-at-once-style difficulty spikes that go just a bit too far. But then another 'What if?' and the world responds, and those frustrations melt away.

According to recent reports, I remember a time in my youth - back before dataminers and FAQs - when video games felt unknowable. Endless enigmas built from creativity and code. It felt like anything could be hiding in there if only you knew where to look, and it was easy to let your imagination run wild. Queen's Domain is so full of secrets, so full of mystery and wonder, it feels like the sort of game my enthusiastic child-brain might have dreamed up all those years ago. 40 hours in, I've seen an ending, but it feels like I'm still far from through. So many mysteries still linger, so many things remain on my checklist of speculative to-dos. Out in the real-world, I've got a Zelda and a GTA awaiting. But it indicates everything about Queen's Domain - this brilliant, vast, deep enigma; this absurdly audacious thing - that I'm still not yet ready to let go.

A copy of Queen's Domain was provided for this review by Future Friends Games.

Samsung just launched a gaming monitor with a refresh rate higher than its price — dual-mode Odyssey G60H offers 1,100 Hz in HD

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samsung's display business has produced some incredible screens, often with groundbreaking features.
  • Sources indicate that if you look at the specifications, you'll see Samsung describe it as a 600Hz gaming monitor.
  • Aside from the resolution and refresh rate specs, this is actually a fairly standard IPS LCD gaming monitor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung's display business has produced some incredible screens, often with groundbreaking features. We have one such example released today: the Samsung Odyssey G60H (LS27HG602ENXZA), a 27" Fast IPS LCD gaming monitor whose standout feature is that it can refresh up to 1,100 times per second. That is 0.91 milliseconds per frame. This exotic screen isn't cheap, but if you're expecting a price to match the max refresh, be surprised, as you can snag it on Amazon for $894.

Sources indicate that if you look at the specifications, you'll see Samsung describe it as a 600Hz gaming monitor. There's no overclocking shenanigans here; this is a "Dual Mode" monitor, meaning that in its native QHD resolution (2560×1440), it supports an already scorching 600Hz refresh rate. You have to slash the resolution by 75% to get that 1100Hz figure, down to just 1280×720, or "HD". Given that this is exactly 1/4 the resolution of QHD, Samsung has hopefully implemented some pretty fancy integer upscaling.

Aside from the resolution and refresh rate specs, this is actually a fairly standard IPS LCD gaming monitor. That's not a knock; it's perfectly fine, with a typical brightness of 400 cd/m², claimed 99% sRGB coverage, rated 1000:1 native contrast, and some measure of HDR10 support—although given the lack of local dimming and the modest brightness, it's hard to call this an HDR display. Naturally, it supports FreeSync Premium and is G-Sync Compatible, and while Samsung doesn't share the VRR ranges, it does say that you can't hit the peak 1,100 refresh rate with FreeSync enabled.

The firm does say that the G60H is the first to include "Odyssey Clear Motion," a feature that it states "reduces motion blur to help players see fast-moving action more clearly during critical moments in gameplay." It's not completely clear what this feature actually is, but Samsung says that "through the optimised blur reduction algorithm, the Odyssey G6 keeps fast-changing scenes clear and crisp.".

Recent findings suggest that samsung notes that it looks to bring the technology to more gaming monitor models, which sounds interesting. Black frame insertion (BFI) and backlight strobing are the two most common methods of motion blur reduction, but Samsung has sold monitors with strobing for over ten years; it would be odd to reintroduce it as a latest feature now.

There's an interesting question hanging over this feature: at 1,100Hz, does a monitor even need dedicated motion blur reduction? Blur Busters has long discussed 1,000Hz as something of a milestone for sample-and-hold displays, arguing that sufficiently high refresh rates can approach the motion clarity of a CRT without requiring backlight strobing.

1,000Hz isn't some magical threshold where motion blur disappears entirely, though. That site's own calculations still predict about one pixel of motion blur for every 1,000 pixels per second of movement at 1ms persistence, and that's assuming instantaneous pixel transitions (like an OLED). At 1,100Hz, that drops to about 0.91 pixels, which is certainly impressive, but not quite zero. The monitor's actual pixel response times also factor into the equation, of course, and Samsung's claimed 1ms GtG response time is actually a measured range of 1.00 to 1.99ms, rounded down to a whole number. I'd be shocked if the real pixel response times weren't more like 3-5ms in the worst case.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Whatever the case with the motion blur feature, in terms of connectivity, the Odyssey G6 can accept video through DisplayPort 2.1 or HDMI 2.1. It has two full-sized HDMI ports, and it also has a USB Type-B connector to pass through its pair of USB Type-A ports to the host machine. Curiously, no USB Type-C connectivity is to be found anywhere, which is unusual on a monitor of this price class, but given that this is clearly aimed at desktop gamers who have the hardware to push games to these kinds of frame rates (at least, with frame generation), it's a sensible omission to be sure, as is the elision of integrated speakers. There is a headphone jack to pass-through HDMI audio, though.

The other crucial characteristics you might like to know are that the Odyssey G6 (G60)'s included stand supports tilt, swivel, pivot, and height adjustments; it supports 100×100 VESA mounting, and that it uses an external AC adaptor, not an internal power supply, which is bad for convenience but good for repairability.

In a recent development, while the image quality is not going to blow you away if you're accustomed to OLEDs, having seen a 540-Hz display in person and been gobsmacked by it, 1,100 Hz sounds absolutely tantalizing. Admittedly, 1280x720 is a low resolution, but we used to play 240p console games on titanic projection TVs. Hardcore competitive gamers don't need high resolutions, so every cut to input lag helps.

This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a latest optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos quickly and accurately.
  • The key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light.
  • Sources indicate that the technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a latest optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos quickly and accurately. Unlike conventional systems that typically examine videos one after another using digital hardware, the UCLA technology can analyze 15 or more video streams at the same time.

The key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light. This allows many videos to be evaluated simultaneously during a single optical pass rather than requiring each one to move separately through a conventional digital processing pipeline.

Sources indicate that the technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight. The researchers designed the optical AI system to serve as a high-throughput, attack-resilient first layer of defense for screening large amounts of manipulated and AI-generated video.

The Growing Challenge of Deepfake Detection.

Rapid improvements in generative AI have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, increasing the need for detection systems that are both accurate and capable of operating at large scale.

It has been revealed that many advanced deepfake detectors depend on enormous amounts of digital computation. A single analysis can require hundreds of billions of floating-point operations, and videos are often processed sequentially. As more content must be checked, both the processing time and energy requirements can rise proportionally.

In a recent development, digital detection systems face another problem. Attackers can deliberately alter fake videos in subtle ways designed to confuse a detector and make manipulated footage appear authentic.

Professor Aydogan Ozcan and his UCLA team developed a hybrid digital-optical system intended to address both challenges.

Sources indicate that A lightweight digital encoder first collects compact information about each video, including spatial, spectral, and temporal features. That information is transformed into a phase pattern and displayed on a programmable spatial light modulator.

The resulting optical wavefront then travels through a free-space-based, passive optical decoder. At the other end, paired optical detectors directly produce an authenticity score for each video.

In effect, the system replaces a computationally demanding digital decoding network with a physical process that can handle many streams in parallel.

Nearly 98% Accuracy Across 15 Videos at Once.

In experiments using visible light, the processor examined 15 Celeb-DF videos simultaneously during each optical pass.

It achieved an average detection accuracy of 97.79%, along with a sensitivity of 99.86% and a specificity of 95.72%. Sensitivity measures how successfully the system identifies manipulated videos, making the particularly high sensitivity important for a screening tool designed to keep fake content from slipping through.

According to recent reports, the 99.86% sensitivity translated to an average false-negative rate of ~0.14%. In other words, only a very small fraction of manipulated videos were incorrectly classified as authentic.

The researchers also pushed the system further by increasing its capacity to 18 videos in a single optical pass. Even at that level, average detection accuracy remained at 96.13%.

More Optical Layers Boost Performance.

The team found that the processor could also become more capable by increasing the physical depth of its passive optical decoder without substantially increasing energy use or inference latency.

When researchers added two optimized passive diffractive layers while testing more difficult deepfake manipulations, detection accuracy improved by ~6.8%.

Sources indicate that these phase-only diffractive layers can be manufactured as passive, static optical structures/surfaces. They perform additional calculations through the diffraction of light, meaning they do not require additional electrical power while the system is performing an inference.

That approach could allow more sophisticated processing without the same energy costs that typically accompany larger digital neural networks.

Testing the System Against Google VEO-3 Videos.

According to recent reports, the researchers did not limit their experiments to conventional face swapping deepfakes. They also challenged the processor with videos produced using Google's VEO-3 model.

Newer generative AI systems can create footage that lacks many of the obvious artifacts associated with earlier deepfake technology, making them a more difficult target for detectors trained primarily on older forms of manipulation.

With only minimal fine-tuning, the optical processor achieved 94.80% accuracy and 97.61% sensitivity on previously unseen VEO-3 videos during experiments.

The results suggest that the approach could potentially adapt as generative AI technology continues to evolve.

A Deepfake Detector Designed to Be Harder to Fool.

The optical system also showed resistance to black-box adversarial attacks and provides inherent protection against white-box attacks.

It has been revealed that part of that security comes from the way the detector physically performs its calculations. Because some of the inference process takes place through diffraction, important parameters of the optical model are effectively embedded within the hardware.

Those parameters can be difficult for an attacker to measure, reproduce, or reverse engineer. That makes reconstructing the detector and designing carefully tailored adversarial changes that can evade it considerably more difficult.

Sources indicate that the processor also continued working reliably when videos were affected by image noise, blur, JPEG compression, and experimental misalignments. According to the researchers, those results illustrate how optical computation could provide a more secure and dependable foundation for some artificial intelligence systems.

A First Line of Defense Against Deepfakes.

Rather than replacing sophisticated digital detectors entirely, the UCLA processor is designed to work as a highly sensitive first stage of a larger detection system.

Massive volumes of video could initially pass through the parallel optical processor. Content identified as suspicious could then be sent to more computationally demanding digital models for a more detailed final assessment.

Such a system could combine the strengths of both approaches. Optical processing could provide parallel operation, low decoder energy requirements, high sensitivity, resistance to adversarial attacks, and the ability to adapt to newer AI video generators, while conventional digital systems could provide deeper analysis when necessary.

The researchers say this combination could eventually be useful for large-scale content moderation, media authentication, surveillance, and other security-critical AI applications.

It has been revealed that the authors of this work are Parnian Ghapandar Kashani and Dr. Shiqi Chen, who contributed equally, and Professor Aydogan Ozcan. The researchers are affiliated with the UCLA Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, the UCLA Bioengineering Department, and the California NanoSystems Institute.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's impossible to have a massive game launch these days without some section of the internet, somewhere, finding grievances with the final product because it does not align with the expectations they had pre-release.

The most recent upset comes in the form of Grand Theft Auto 6's revised take on, well, grand theft auto. In case you're one of the few still unfamiliar, grand theft auto is more than the titular moniker for Rockstar's premier crime simulation series; it's actually a US legal term for the act of stealing or attempting to steal a motor vehicle. In most previous GTA entries, this was a central part of the core gameplay loop: accept a mission, nick a car, complete the mission, nick another car, getaway. It's an endemic part of the loop, and has become so popular and identifiable as such that even other games - Watch Dogs, Saint's Row, Cyberpunk 2077, and so on - have emulated the mechanic.

So it makes sense that the internet is in a bit of a spin about GTA 6's more mature and restrained take on its eponymous crime. A quick, no-frills getaway in a vehicle you've hijacked on the road isn't always the most effective option. A mindless crime spree on the streets of Leonida is not a simple thing to pull off, nor an easy thing to live down. In this game, actions have consequences, and an ill-timed or ill-judged car jacking can promptly and efficiently put an end to your criminal ambitions.

In a recent development, that's not to say you cannot simply steal cars. Of course you can: the option to saunter up to an occupied vehicle and jack it from its registered owner is available to you from the very beginning of the game. But the citizens of Leonida aren't going to take your wanton act of foolishness lying down; many of the motorists in the county will fight back, pull a piece on you, or run you over mid-robbery attempt. Even if you are lucky to find one of the more pliant residents of the city, you might find something peculiar is happening in their car. I jacked a woman in the city over the weekend, and the cat she was ferrying from place to place decided to attack me, causing me to crash. I've heard other people say they've had muffled cries coming from the boot of the car where someone is transporting a hostage, or incidents where they've jacked the same person multiple times, leading to the poor car's owner to have a breakdown in the middle of the city.

That cat event, the team here at Eurogamer has worked out, is an early game trigger - it seems stealing random cars early in the game will increase the chance of this encounter occurring. Rockstar's guiding hand is more visible here, then, in trying to teach you a lesson: don't steal cars. You're given your own - Jason's two-door coupé utility, a Vapid Creado - that I actually formed quite an emotional bond with in the opening 10-or-so hours of the game. 'Look after this car,' Rockstar insists, tutorialising you how to repair it, customise it, make it all pretty so it's in good condition when you go pick up Lucia for the first time.

According to recent reports, shortly after the 10 hour marker, narrative events whisk you away elsewhere and you're given a 'slim jim', a long, thin tool that allows you to break into locked cars - something you could only do with a quick elbow jab before. The benefit here is two-fold; you can break into cars without setting off their alarms, and without breaking glass and lowering their resale value (something quite vital in the earlier sections of the game). So, it takes you until Chapter 2 to start being able to more reliably and consistently break into vehicles. Good.

And it'll take even longer to break into keyless vehicles. We're in 2026 after all, and it's heavily implied this is when GTA 6 is also set - it stands to reason that many cars run keyless fobs, and your old-school tools won't cut it if you want to break into a Zorruso, rather than an old Vapid truck. But then, even when you're well-armed and ready to start an illustrious new career as Vice City's most nefarious car thief, there's more to consider. Most modern cars also come with trackers: standard trackers simply prevent you modding cars you don't own (not an issue you'll face very often), but advanced trackers are more problematic.

Sources indicate that boosting a car with an advanced tracker immediately alerts the cops to your location, and they close in on you fast. The only answer to this problem is flooring it, and outspeeding the signal ping the tracker is sending out: you need to drive fast and cleanly in order to stay mobile long enough for the tracker to deactivate, and this often incurs damage that makes selling these cars to fences a less viable option. You can't even sell cars with trackers installed at all to some fences until you're much, much further into the game.

Recent findings suggest that so, long story short, stealing cars is a faff in GTA 6. But I like that. I like that Rockstar has evolved the gameplay formula to more accurately reflect the state of the world in 2026. Modern problems require modern answers, and given that Rockstar has gone above and beyond in its creation of a sandbox simulation of Florida, I feel the immersion would be broken by just being able to saunter up to any car you want and break into it. No, needing a 'slim jim' or a key cloner - or needing to case my victims properly before trying to jack them - makes for a better game as far as I'm concerned. It makes me roleplay Jason and Lucia better, it makes me engage with the game's systems more, it makes me appreciate the cars that I do have whilst I have them.

It also improves the flow of the game and how I interact with missions. I recently played GTA: Vice City, and after most missions were wrapped up, I would simply fling the nearest motorist onto the sidewalk, hop in their car, and drive away into the Malibu-styled sunset. I can't simply do that in GTA 6: I need to think about my getaway options, whether there's heat on my car, and where my next best (and cheapest) ride is going to be if a robbery or raid goes awry. 'Ah,' I think, 'I understand why there's a garage next to that safehouse on the map now.'.

In making the act of grand theft auto harder and more awkward, Rockstar has nudged me into playing Grand Theft Auto the game like a more thoughtful criminal. I play it like someone on the run, who wouldn't just be indiscriminately committing wanton acts of felony theft on a whim, just because I didn't want to run four blocks down the road to meet my pals for a drink. It's a gorgeous example of functionality, design, and narrative dovetailing - one of the key reasons this is a five star game. The complaints about the system, to my ear, don't reflect what Rockstar has built here. Plus, if it bothers you that much, you could always try to play GTA 6 like a mindless thug if you really want to - just expect the world to treat you like one, too.

Tech Report: Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 captures the franchise's bloody absurdity like nothing else

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, warhammer 40,000 is a universe of two distinct moods.
  • It has been revealed that perhaps the best praise I can give Boltgun 2 - which, like its 2023 predecessor, is developed by Auroch Digital - is that it honours 40k's sillier side wonderfully.
  • Sources indicate that like its predecessor, Boltgun 2 adopts the style of a retro first-person shooter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, warhammer 40,000 is a universe of two distinct moods. On the one hand, it's a grimdark future of serious, solemn stories where trillions die in galactic wars of attrition; of tragedies and insurmountable threats. But there's also the other side of Warhammer 40,000, where goofy hilarity and gory absurdity lies. Where Orks paint their cars go-faster red, and where chainaxe-wielding Khorne Berserkers indulge in gleeful hyperviolence.

It has been revealed that perhaps the best praise I can give Boltgun 2 - which, like its 2023 predecessor, is developed by Auroch Digital - is that it honours 40k's sillier side wonderfully. It's unashamedly gory, over-the-top, and, most crucially, fun. Its creators understand that after a long day at work, sometimes all you want to do is shred a guy or five.

Sources indicate that like its predecessor, Boltgun 2 adopts the style of a retro first-person shooter. It's a little bit Doom, a little bit Duke Nukem, as you blast through its low-poly environments and its sprite-based enemies, hoovering up - and using up - ammo and health as you go. I jumped in right as I was starting World of Warcraft: Forever. And in contrast to that game's slow burn beginning, Boltgun 2 is a full-throttle roar right from the word go that rarely lets up. Just moments in, you're belting down corridors - either playing as a Space Marine or a Sister of Battle, depending on your mood - and unloading endless rounds into cultists and Chaos dregs.

I should note that while I'm a Warhammer fan, the original Boltgun passed me by, so this sequel has been something of a revelation. It truly revels in its violent delights, indulging in its hunger for spectacle. As your bullets turn lesser goons into raspberry jam, strong animation work and excellent audio design bring its cartoonish brutality to life. And it's paired with some brilliantly over-the-top weaponry too. Take your basic Boltgun: when you pull the trigger, this beefed-up rifle's fist-sized projectiles erupt with a weighty bang. Weaker enemies get minced in their path, and for the Space Marine, this is the first gun.

It has been revealed that as a Space Marine, you've also got a devastating cool-down-based rush attack known as the Obliterating Charge. It's handy for repositioning in a pinch, but it also bursts through enemies with the power of a speeding lorry. The Space Marine has his chainsword for slice-and-dicing too, and tougher enemies really require some elbow grease - you really have to mash that melee button - to get through 'em. Is all this the height of video game sophistication? Absolutely not, but it got me grinning, and it's a visceral thrill that still hasn't lost its sheen.

I also love that the two selectable characters aren't just cosmetic swaps. If you opt for the Sister of Battle, she comes with her own distinct weapons and abilities. I adore her Flamer and the close-quarters havoc it can cause; the way fire roars from its nozzle as sparks fly and black smoke spews. And while she doesn't have an Obliterating Charge, she does get a slide move that's a fantastic way to maintain forward-momentum. Both characters have their own quirks and appeal - the Space Marine is slower and heavier, but offers punchier gunplay, while the Sister of Battle is swifter but lighter in combat - and both, I reckon, warrant their own playthroughs.

It'd also be remiss not to mention Boltgun 2's dedicated 'taunt' button. Both characters have their own voice lines and many are context-specific. It's a fun thing to spam mid-fight, or to hit when celebrating moments of especially grisly victory. I remembered hearing you could get some extra ammo or healing items if you threw a taunt at the floating servo skull that flies beside you throughout the game and, yup, it's true. Little details like that, alongside the smaller secrets hidden around each mission, create an FPS that's so far been a real joy to mess around in.

It's occasionally all a bit floaty, perhaps, but the combination of speed and action is a winner. What elevates it even further, though, are those Warhammer 40,000 flourishes. I've been amazed how swiftly levels introduce upcoming enemies, and how lovingly they're depicted here. Basic Black Legion Chaos Space Marines take centre stage early on, but as you progress, new subfactions are introduced with their own unique quirks. Khorne-loving Berserkers thunder toward you at speed for painful melee strikes, while devilish Bloodletters lurch at your blind spots with giant swords in-hand. In a later mission things are flipped, and the melee-focused enemies are replaced by menacing ranged forces. Noise Marines carry giant sonic weapons that shoot from afar and disrupt your movement, all while their own daemon allies leap in.

Sources indicate that there's also something to say about the variety of the missions you'll encounter. Often, you're given a choice of paths through the game, each with their own planets and battlegrounds. These can be snow-laden ruins, unruly jungles, or cities under siege, and things get even wilder the further you go into the game. And while it's not the sort of experience that encourages you to stand still, if you do you'll see some striking views.

There's a moment, not too far into Boltgun 2, when you find yourself in the bowels of a Khorne-controlled world. Here, literal rivers of blood flow, and you can't go two steps without someone or something rushing in. So I whip out a shotgun and charge on in, properly exhilarated by the chaos of it all as I blast stray enemies into mist. It takes a lot to stave off fatigue in a game with this sort of relentless action but Auroch manages it here.

Warhammer 40,000 is, I think, the sort of setting you can't do half-heartedly, and Boltgun 2 feels like a total embrace of the series' wilder, more absurd side. So far, around five hours in, it's a damn good FPS, retro or otherwise. You can grab it for just over £20, and it's even on sale as of writing. For that price it's a no-brainer.
