General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Utah asks to drop criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.
  • Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.
  • The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance.” Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise. The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance.” Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there. “Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown said in a statement. Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court. The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity. The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its cofounders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on December 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case. Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown’s office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling. Utah’s felony charges represented a latest tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. Brown’s office also has asked a court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah. Kalshi, the nation’s largest prediction market operator, said Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) wouldn’t immediately stop Utah’s attempts to shut it down there. A Kalshi spokeswoman called it an “unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi” but said the company will continue to fight in court for the right to operate in Utah. Kalshi, like the CFTC, argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 44 other states have opposed that view. Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request, and an appeal is pending. Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi. —By Marc Levy, Associated Press.

Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.

The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance.” Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there.

“Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown stated in a statement.

Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court.

The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.

The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its cofounders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on December 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case.

Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown’s office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling.

Recent findings suggest that utah’s felony charges represented a newly introduced tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. Brown’s office also has asked a court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah.

Kalshi, the nation’s largest prediction market operator, mentioned Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) wouldn’t immediately stop Utah’s attempts to shut it down there.

A Kalshi spokeswoman called it an “unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi” but said the organization will continue to fight in court for the right to operate in Utah.

Kalshi, like the CFTC, argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 44 other states have opposed that view.

In a recent development, kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request, and an appeal is pending.

Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi.

Tech Report: Elon Musk once again promises Tesla’s fresh autonomous driving is better than humans

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, elon Musk has a new promise: Version 15 of Full Self-Driving drives better than a real driver.
  • Elon Musk has a new promise: Version 15 of Full Self-Driving drives better than a real driver.
  • It was great news back in November 2023, too, when he wrote: “Over time, Version 12 (end-to-end neural nets) will far exceed human safety even when unsupervised.” Also in August 2025, when he noted: “v14 will be better than human for sure, but I don’t know if it will be 10X.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, elon Musk has a new promise: Version 15 of Full Self-Driving drives better than a real driver. “Completely new architecture that deserves being called ‘super’ intelligence, as it drives better than human intelligence,” he wrote on X after Tesla started sending the update to a first batch of owners. That’s great news. It was great news back in November 2023, too, when he wrote: “Over time, Version 12 (end-to-end neural nets) will far exceed human safety even when unsupervised.” Also in August 2025, when he said: “v14 will be better than human for sure, but I don’t know if it will be 10X. Maybe 2X to 3X. v15 has a shot at 10X.” Back then, he offered no data, and no third-party study to support his claim. It’s the same thing now. Tesla states that the new FSD v15—which Musk expects to roll out widely in December—upgrades the neural network that processes the camera sensors into information for the car to drive. It has also swapped the old lo-fi grayscale schematic 3D view for an AI-generated live street scene that looks GTA VI-ish. The latter is the only thing that we know is real—and I have to admit it looks pretty neat—but nobody knows if the new driving engine works as well as Musk claims. [Image: Tesla] Same song, new version number It may not matter too much. The new v15 is still Level 2 autonomous driving, which means drivers will need to watch the road at all times. While Musk says it drives better than a human, it must be a very dumb human because Tesla’s own support page says the software “does not make the vehicle autonomous” and is meant for use “only with a fully attentive driver.” That matters because when a person has to be ready to take over the wheel at any second, every avoided crash is just as much a win for the human as for the machine. FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network Safety25x better handling of safety critical casesTesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to doNavigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW— Tesla (@Tesla) November 21, 2026 Tesla claims that the new FSD offers “25x better handling of safety critical cases.” Better than what? Phil Duan, who leads self-driving at Tesla, said on X that “v15 is 25x safer than v14 across the fleet.” Musk answered an X user, too: “Some people thought we meant 25% improvement; no we mean 25 times!” But we don’t really know about how much “safer” v14 was either. As electric mobility site Electrek points out, without real published figures or a peer-reviewed study—like this one on Waymo reducing its crashes with injured people by 85%—that “25x” claim is hard to substantiate. In a post, the company explains that its new vision encoder—the part of the network that interprets the information from the car’s video cameras—is the reason for that “25x better handling.” Now shared by FSD, Robotaxis, and Optimus humanoids, the engineering team says the new software improves “the critical intervention rate by 25x.” Tesla says the new encoder was trained on “millions of internet videos.” According to Tesla, v15 adjusts its speed better in bad weather and school zones, steers clear of deep standing water, and is quicker to spot signs, potholes, small animals, chains, and junk on the road. It doesn’t say anything about fake Looney Tunes-painted tunnels. It can ease off for speed cameras, too. And it learns from you, so if you cancel the slowdown at the same speed camera twice, by accelerating, it will stop braking at that point of the road. The company also claims that the car’s interior camera—which checks if you are paying attention to the road or not—now works more often when you wear hats and sunglasses. Neat! As part of the update, Tesla Reality View has changed. It now looks very similar to the live situational awareness screens you get in some Chinese cars: a hyperrealistic view of the road and your car as seen from behind at a 45-degree angle. You can see vehicles and people in 3D hyperrealistic renderings. Even the buildings are textured and lit like the real thing. It feels like a high-end car racing game. Musk claims “it’s like GTA.” It looks neat, but it doesn’t seem to convey information better than the older user interface (UI), which showed a much clearer representation of reality. Seen from a high angle, it was a simplified, very stylized version of the road populated with semitransparent versions of vehicles and nearby people. In the old version, despite its perception problems, it was easy to get instant situational awareness. In the new v15, the realism obscures the information with too much darkness and glitz. The interface also features a blue ribbon that traces the route FSD intends to drive, so you can correct it. Chevron arrows float overhead before every turn. And the map now shows several parking spots at your destination. Some Chinese car manufacturers are already displaying this information directly on the windshield, projecting computer-generated wide-screen augmented-reality (AR) graphics over the real world. Fortunately, you can switch to a split view or just pick the GPS map view. Musk claims “you can tap any point on the reality revisualizer to make your car go there.”  Musk says that the new UI uses the same visual features the FSD v15 driving model uses: It’s all AI-generated. The AI model renders short bursts of eight frames at 36 frames per second, using just half of one of the accelerators in the car’s AI4 computer. Still, the video may lag behind reality because the AI is not fast enough. Musk admits the lag is “a bit high due to compute constraints.” He claims Tesla has a way to trim it by about 35%. More promises. If December’s wide release arrives on time (which may or may not happen), it will put the new FSD in a lot more hands. In 2027 we will be able to test the real value of Musk’s promises once again. Let’s stay positive. Maybe this will be it. You know what they say: 15th time’s the charm.

Elon Musk has a new promise: Version 15 of Full Self-Driving drives better than a real driver. “Completely new architecture that deserves being called ‘super’ intelligence, as it drives better than human intelligence,” he wrote on X after Tesla started sending the update to a first batch of owners.

That’s great news.

It was great news back in November 2023, too, when he wrote: “Over time, Version 12 (end-to-end neural nets) will far exceed human safety even when unsupervised.” Also in August 2025, when he noted: “v14 will be better than human for sure, but I don’t know if it will be 10X. Maybe 2X to 3X. v15 has a shot at 10X.” Back then, he offered no data, and no third-party study to support his claim. It’s the same thing now.

The latter is the only thing that we know is real—and I have to admit it looks pretty neat—but nobody knows if the new driving engine works as well as Musk claims.

It may not matter too much. The upcoming v15 is still Level 2 autonomous driving, which means drivers will need to watch the road at all times. While Musk claims it drives better than a human, it must be a very dumb human because Tesla’s own support page says the software “does not make the vehicle autonomous” and is meant for use “only with a fully attentive driver.” That matters because when a person has to be ready to take over the wheel at any second, every avoided crash is just as much a win for the human as for the machine.

FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network Safety25x better handling of safety critical casesTesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to doNavigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW.

Tesla claims that the newly introduced FSD offers “25x better handling of safety critical cases.” Better than what? Phil Duan, who leads self-driving at Tesla, remarked on X that “v15 is 25x safer than v14 across the fleet.” Musk answered an X user, too: “Some people thought we meant 25% improvement; no we mean 25 times!” But we don’t really know about how much “safer” v14 was either. As electric mobility site Electrek points out, without real published figures or a peer-reviewed study—like this one on Waymo reducing its crashes with injured people by 85%—that “25x” claim is hard to substantiate.

In a post, the company explains that its latest vision encoder—the part of the network that interprets the information from the car’s video cameras—is the reason for that “25x better handling.” Now shared by FSD, Robotaxis, and Optimus humanoids, the engineering team says the new software improves “the critical intervention rate by 25x.” Tesla says the new encoder was trained on “millions of internet videos.”.

According to recent reports, according to Tesla, v15 adjusts its speed better in bad weather and school zones, steers clear of deep standing water, and is quicker to spot signs, potholes, small animals, chains, and junk on the road. It doesn’t say anything about fake Looney Tunes-painted tunnels.

Sources indicate that it can ease off for speed cameras, too. And it learns from you, so if you cancel the slowdown at the same speed camera twice, by accelerating, it will stop braking at that point of the road. The organization also claims that the car’s interior camera—which checks if you are paying attention to the road or not—now works more often when you wear hats and sunglasses.

Recent findings suggest that as part of the enhancement, Tesla Reality View has changed. It now looks very similar to the live situational awareness screens you get in some Chinese cars: a hyperrealistic view of the road and your car as seen from behind at a 45-degree angle. You can see vehicles and people in 3D hyperrealistic renderings. Even the buildings are textured and lit like the real thing. It feels like a high-end car racing game. Musk claims “it’s like GTA.”.

It looks neat, but it doesn’t seem to convey information better than the older user interface (UI), which revealed a much clearer representation of reality. Seen from a high angle, it was a simplified, very stylized version of the road populated with semitransparent versions of vehicles and nearby people. In the old version, despite its perception problems, it was easy to get instant situational awareness. In the latest v15, the realism obscures the information with too much darkness and glitz.

The interface also features a blue ribbon that traces the route FSD intends to drive, so you can correct it. Chevron arrows float overhead before every turn. And the map now demonstrates several parking spots at your destination. Some Chinese car manufacturers are already displaying this information directly on the windshield, projecting computer-generated wide-screen augmented-reality (AR) graphics over the real world.

Industry observers note that fortunately, you can switch to a split view or just pick the GPS map view. Musk claims “you can tap any point on the reality revisualizer to make your car go there.”.

Musk notes that the latest UI uses the same visual features the FSD v15 driving model uses: It’s all AI-generated. The AI model renders short bursts of eight frames at 36 frames per second, using just half of one of the accelerators in the car’s AI4 computer.

Sources indicate that still, the video may lag behind reality because the AI is not fast enough. Musk admits the lag is “a bit high due to compute constraints.” He claims Tesla has a way to trim it by about 35%. More promises.

In a recent development, if December’s wide release arrives on time (which may or may not happen), it will put the fresh FSD in a lot more hands. In 2027 we will be able to test the real value of Musk’s promises once again. Let’s stay positive. Maybe this will be it. You know what they say: 15th time’s the charm.

According to recent reports, google designed TPUs from the ground up to be exceptionally efficient for machine learning workloads, delivering top-tier performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). Because TPUs trade general-purpose hardware scheduling for wide systolic arrays, dedicated SparseCore engines, and custom interconnect fabrics, adhering to specific architectural best practices is essential to achieve maximum performance. To help developers get the most out of TPUs, we are launching the open-source AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide. This post highlights its key principles—spanning shape alignment, architectural choices like LatentMoE, and parallelism strategies—to accelerate LLMs, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and other hardware-intensive workloads on TPUs.

Performance tuning starts with model definition. Architectural choices made before the first training step set permanent ceilings on MFU (Model FLOP Utilization), cost, and serving latency. This guide gives concrete, hardware-grounded design rules for teams building or adapting models for TPUs, organized into three groups:.

Industry observers note that how to use this guide. The shape rules apply to anyone designing a fresh model. If you are adapting an existing model rather than designing one, the Expressing Parallelism section applies without touching the checkpoint. The general rules hold for any large-matmul architecture (dense LLMs, multimodal, and world models), and the companion AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign repository grows model- and workload-specific sections over time.

Industry observers note that eighth-generation TPUs. These principles carry forward to TPU 8t and TPU 8i and to the newly announced TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max. The reasoning stays the same and the thresholds move with the hardware. TPU 8t and TPU 8i both add native FP4. For training, TPU 8t also brings more balanced Vector Processing Unit (VPU) scaling. For serving, TPU 8i adds the Boardfly topology, a Collectives Acceleration Engine (CAE), and 3x more on-chip SRAM. We note the effects inline in Principles 5–8, and follow-up posts will cover eighth-generation designs in depth.

Sources indicate that measured evidence. Alongside the published sources, notes marked Measured carry results from our own Ironwood profiling program: open 20–30B MoEs (a Qwen3-30B-derived LatentMoE variant; GPT-OSS-20B) plus dense controls, single slice (except for the 512-chip TPU v7x and 1,024-chip TPU v4 ablations in Principle 4), BF16, training shapes up to 32K sequence, all against tuned-systems baselines. Treat the trends and rankings as transferable, the exact percentages as config-specific.

In a recent development, TPUs are purpose-built custom ML ASICs designed from the ground up to deliver state-of-the-art performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). While their architectural choices—such as wide 256×256 systolic arrays, software-managed VMEM, dedicated SparseCore engines, and direct multi-dimensional ICI fabrics—enable exceptional efficiency, they inherently create specific structural constraints and programming patterns that must be carefully followed to unlock maximal performance. Reaching peak efficiency requires aligning model shapes, routing, and parallelism directly with these underlying hardware characteristics:.

In a recent development, generating a single AI video clip is easy now. You send a prompt and get a few seconds of footage back. The trouble starts when the goal is three, five, or ten minutes of video where the same character looks the same in every scene, the style does not drift, and the captions line up with the picture.

Recent findings suggest that most guides stop at the clip. This one covers the part after it, treating a video as a small build pipeline: a storyboard that is data, prompts generated from that data, clips normalised and stitched with ffmpeg, and captions derived from the same source. If you want to wire a generation model into your own application first, SitePoint's guide to integrating generative video APIs into web applications covers the request and webhook side. If the finished video is headed to a YouTube channel, how to get a YouTube API key and use the Data API is a good starting point for the publishing side. Everything between those two is below.

Long-form AI video fails at the seams between clips, not inside them. Strategy for continuity before you generate anything.

A storyboard stored as JSON can be validated, versioned, diffed, and turned into prompts by code, which a pile of loose prompts cannot.

It has been revealed that repeat the full character description in every prompt. Models do not remember the previous clip.

According to recent reports, clips from different generations rarely share resolution, frame rate, or codec settings. Normalise them before joining.

Captions are cheapest when generated from the script and measured clip durations, not transcribed afterwards.

Industry observers note that current video models generate short clips, commonly a handful of seconds each. A longer video is therefore many clips, and every clip is an independent generation. The model has no memory of what the character wore in the previous one.

It has been revealed that that produces three kinds of failure. The character drifts, so hair, clothing, or proportions change between scenes. The style drifts, so lighting and colour grade shift from cut to cut. And the technical specs drift, so one clip is 24 frames per second at one resolution and the next is something else. Each of these is fixable, but only if the project is organised so the fixes can be applied consistently.

Industry observers note that start with a structured storyboard instead of a document full of prompts. One file holds the style, a "character bible", and an ordered list of scenes.

"project": "rainy-day-lantern",.

"style": "soft watercolor picture book illustration, warm evening light, 16:9",.

"mira": "a nine year old girl with short curly black hair, a yellow raincoat and red rubber boots",.

"lantern": "a small round paper lantern with a gentle orange glow and a tiny smiling face".

"setting": "a narrow cobblestone street in light rain",.

"action": "walks slowly past closed shops, looking up at the sky",.

"camera": "slow push in from a medium shot",.

"narration": "It had rained all afternoon, and the street was quiet.".

"characters": ["mira", "lantern"],.

"setting": "under a bakery awning",.

"action": "finds the lantern glowing on a wooden crate and kneels beside it",.

"camera": "static medium close up",.

"narration": "Then she noticed something glowing under the awning.".

Recent findings suggest that because it is data, a script can check it before you spend any generation credits. Two checks pay for themselves quickly: every character named in a scene must exist in the bible, and no scene may be longer than the clip limit of the model you use.

${scene.id}: ${scene.duration}s is over the ${MAX_CLIP_SECONDS}s clip limit, split it into shots.

Treat MAX_CLIP_SECONDS as a setting. Limits differ between models and change over time, so check the one you are using rather than trusting the number in this example.

Never write the per-scene prompt by hand. Generate it, so the style line and the character descriptions are identical every time.

The character description appears word for word in every scene that includes that character. This is the single most effective consistency tactic that needs no special tooling. Changing a detail, say the colour of the boots, becomes one edit in the bible instead of a search through twenty prompts, and the diff reveals exactly what changed between versions.

Put the style line first and keep it identical across all scenes.

It has been revealed that describe one action per clip. Two sequential actions in one prompt often produce a blend of both.

Sources indicate that keep camera directions simple. A single move per clip is more reliable than a combination.

Avoid naming real people, brands, or existing characters in prompts. Beyond the rights issue, it makes results harder to reproduce.

Recent findings suggest that clips from separate generations often disagree on resolution, frame rate, pixel format, or codec parameters. Joining them directly can produce stutters, green frames, or an outright error. Convert every clip to one agreed format first.

-vf "scale=1280:720:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease,pad=1280:720:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,fps=24,format=yuv420p" \.

-an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 "norm/$(basename "$f")".

In a recent development, the filter scales each clip to fit a 1280 by 720 frame, adds padding if the aspect ratio differs, sets 24 frames per second, and forces a widely compatible pixel format. The -an flag drops any audio the model generated, since narration will be added as one track later. Name clips with zero padded numbers such as s01.mp4 and s02.mp4, so a shell glob sorts them in story order.

Once every file shares the same parameters, the concat demuxer can join them without re-encoding:.

for f in norm/*.mp4; do echo "file '$PWD/$f'"; done > list.txt.

ffmpeg -y -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy stitched.mp4.

Sources indicate that hard cuts are the safe default. Crossfades are possible with ffmpeg's xfade filter, but they require careful offset arithmetic and a re-encode, so add them only when a cut genuinely looks wrong.

It has been revealed that captions are easiest when they come from the script, not from a speech recognition pass over the finished video. The storyboard already holds the narration text and each scene's length, so an SRT file is a few lines of code. Use measured durations rather than planned ones, because a generated clip is often a little shorter or longer than requested.

return Number(out.toString().trim());.

const ms = Math.round(totalSeconds * 1000);.

const h = String(Math.floor(ms / 3600000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const m = String(Math.floor((ms % 3600000) / 60000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const s = String(Math.floor((ms % 60000) / 1000)).padStart(2, '0');.

const rest = String(ms % 1000).padStart(3, '0');.

Recent findings suggest that patch each scene's duration from measureSeconds on the normalised clip before calling buildSrt. If a narration line is long, split it across two caption blocks so it stays readable. Then combine picture, voiceover, and captions in one final step:.

ffmpeg -y -i stitched.mp4 -i narration.mp3 -i captions.srt \.

-c:v copy -c:a aac -c:s mov_text -shortest final.mp4.

Soft captions like these can be switched off by the viewer and read by assistive technology, which is better than burning text into the picture. Keep the .srt file as well, since most platforms accept it as a separate upload.

According to recent reports, everything above is a good fit when you need repeatability: many videos from templates, versioned storyboards, automated publishing, or tight control over the model. The price is that you own the glue code, the ffmpeg settings, and the failures.

According to recent reports, for one off projects, or when the people making the video are not developers, a managed platform is often the more sensible choice. Tools such as magiclight.ai bundle story to video generation, character handling, voice, and an editor in one interface, and advertise videos of up to 50 minutes. Check the specifics yourself, because claims like that are marketing, and results depend on your content. One point matters for developers in particular: if you need to automate generation from your own code, confirm that the platform you pick offers an API or export route before you build a workflow around it. A tool with a good editor and no programmatic access suits a different job than the pipeline in this article.

A short manual pass catches what automation does not. Watch the whole video once at normal speed, looking only at continuity. Read the captions against the audio. Check that no real person's likeness, brand mark, or protected character slipped into the footage. Finally, check the disclosure rules of the platform you publish on, since many now ask creators to label realistic synthetic media, and the rules change.

Industry observers note that the model is only one component of a long-form AI video. The reliability comes from the structure around it: a validated storyboard, prompts generated from it, clips forced into one format, and captions derived from measured data. Each of those is ordinary software engineering, and none of it depends on which generation model you choose, so the pipeline survives when the model changes.

Start with a two minute video and four or five scenes. Fix the seams there before scaling up, because every continuity problem you find at that size is one you will not have to hunt for in a ten minute project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts. Even the stock price took a bit of a dip after surging by over 30% on Monday. Within the company, however, the mood appears to be considerably lighter. In videos circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls and staircases as they cheered for him. Between chants of “Jensen! Jensen!” and “We love you Jensen,” he addressed his staff in a display of contrition. “I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this,” he stated. “I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” After an employee threw her arms around Huang in a tight hug—lasting over 10 seconds—he continued: “Thank you all for the second chance. I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.” Many Nvidia employees have taken to LinkedIn to express their relief over Huang’s return, seemingly overlooking the indiscretions that led to his ousting. They heaped praise on their newly reinstated CEO, describing him as the “heartbeat of Nvidia” and “one of a kind.”  One employee even invoked Charles Dickens, paraphrasing the opening of A Tale of Two Cities: “It was the worst of times, it is the best of times. It was the season of Darkness, it is the season of Light. It was the winter of despair, it is the spring of hope. We had nothing before us, we have everything before us.” Another employee claimed he always knew Huang would return to Nvidia: “When Jensen stepped down, many said their goodbyes and thanked him for his legacy. I stayed quiet—not out of indifference, but because deep down I knew there is only one boss, and he would be back.” A former robotics engineer at Nvidia who quit rather publicly after Huang’s resignation congratulated him and admitted he made a hasty decision. “Looking back, I may have moved too promptly, and I don’t want to rush into another major decision. For now, I’d like to take some time to rest, reflect, and think carefully about my future. As part of that, I’m open to exploring the possibility of returning.” These reactions line up with previous reports about employee sentiment after Huang stepped down: According to Wired, many employees showed immediate support for him internally, asking the board to reverse the decision. More than 10,000 current Nvidia employees, or about a quarter of its workforce, signed a petition to reinstate Huang as CEO. Still, there are some employees who seem to feel differently—perhaps those who have been the target of Huang’s outbursts and creative insults, as reported by the Newly introduced York Times recently. In a Wired report this week, several current and former employees expressed frustration over the turn of events, in part because they had hoped Huang’s exit would usher in some long overdue changes. A number of employees were disturbed by Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy and at least one inappropriate relationship with an employee. Beyond that, however, they also felt that Nvidia condoned abusive behavior and echoed previous claims that Huang belittled employees at times. (In an internal post, one employee asserted: “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”) Workers also told Wired that the focus on unity and the “one team” ethos discouraged employees from challenging leadership. Even employees who have few misgivings about the culture may now find themselves questioning Huang’s leadership. One engineering leader openly grappled with his feelings about Huang in a LinkedIn post, before he was reinstated. “Some believe his contributions to NVIDIA and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” he wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. I’ve wrestled with this question all week. My opinion has probably changed every single day. And I’ve realized something. I don’t have a clear answer.” As evidenced by the reception to Huang yesterday, this may not be the prevailing view among employees. But whether or not other employees have lost faith in Huang, there are now open questions about how—if at all—the company prepares to address the myriad complications that have been exposed by the events of the last few weeks.

In a Wired report this week, several current and former employees expressed frustration over the turn of events, in part because they had hoped Huang’s exit would usher in some long overdue changes. A number of employees were disturbed by Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy and at least one inappropriate relationship with an employee.

Industry observers note that beyond that, however, they also felt that Nvidia condoned abusive behavior and echoed previous claims that Huang belittled employees at times. (In an internal post, one employee asserted: “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”) Workers also told Wired that the focus on unity and the “one team” ethos discouraged employees from challenging leadership.

Even employees who have few misgivings about the culture may now find themselves questioning Huang’s leadership. One engineering leader openly grappled with his feelings about Huang in a LinkedIn post, before he was reinstated. “Some believe his contributions to NVIDIA and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” he wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. I’ve wrestled with this question all week. My opinion has probably changed every single day. And I’ve realized something. I don’t have a clear answer.”.

As evidenced by the reception to Huang yesterday, this may not be the prevailing view among employees. But whether or not other employees have lost faith in Huang, there are now open questions about how—if at all—the manufacturer looks to address the myriad problems that have been exposed by the events of the last few weeks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders.
  • Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders.
  • In a survey conducted shortly after the midterm elections, 82% of Americans noted they prefer leaders who “get things back to normal rather than shake things up” and 82% also said they prefer a “stable and predictable” life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders. But these days, at least, Americans are yearning for some stability. In a survey conducted shortly after the midterm elections, 82% of Americans stated they prefer leaders who “get things back to normal rather than shake things up” and 82% also said they prefer a “stable and predictable” life. The global public relations firm Burson interviewed about 1,600 Americans across party lines. The poll was published November 14. Ninety percent of respondents also said they want honest, calm, consistent leadership (90%), and 75% said they lose respect for CEOs who change positions under pressure. It is easy to interpret these findings as a reflection of current public opinion about President Donald Trump. Trump’s penchant for disruption and brash businessman image helped him win the White House twice, but the outcome of the midterms—and the results of the Burson survey—indicate that the public has grown tired of the chaos. A survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters found that about two-thirds thought Trump had the wrong priorities, while seven in 10 said Congress hasn’t been doing enough to check the president’s power. As Fast Firm reported earlier this month, the midterm results also illustrate the risks organizations run when they become overly dependent on a charismatic leader. A leader’s success can make subordinates increasingly reluctant to question their judgment, even when circumstances change. “At some point, you have to ask whether people are following your vision, or simply afraid to challenge it,” leadership expert Adam Mendler said.

Streaming in 1080p will be the default in Google Meet, regardless of whether you pay for Google Workspace. That includes personal Google Accounts.

Sources indicate that google states people will default to sending and receiving 1080p video, at the minimum. Previously, Google Meet made 720p the standard for streaming, and a higher resolution had historically been locked behind the Google One 2TB plan. The only requirement to stream your own 1080p video in Google Meet for web will be hardware-based. Google’s press release states that devices with cameras capable of streaming in high definition will do so, and the feature will be turned on automatically.

Sources indicate that it can be disabled, though. People can head to Settings > Video in Google Meet for web. Video will also appear in a lower resolution if the user’s video tile is shrunk down on-screen.

In a recent development, the upgrade appears to be centered on web-only instances of Google Meet, and might not include the app on Android or iOS. For the time being, those versions may still be limited to streaming in 720p for those who don’t have an active Google One subscription.

Google Meet started its extended rollout of 1080p streaming to everyone earlier this month, so it shouldn’t be much longer until the change has taken place completely.

  • Industry observers note that the White House recently confirmed the formation of a “tiger team” dedicated to preventing major mess-ups like the recent multi-hour ground stop, which snarled airports nationwide as a mountain of delayed and rescheduled flights piled up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that recent chaos is making Americans wary of braving air travel this holiday season, but the Trump administration notes it has a plan. The White House recently declared the formation of a “tiger team” dedicated to preventing major mess-ups like the recent multi-hour ground stop, which snarled airports nationwide as a mountain of delayed and rescheduled flights piled up. The mid-November incident lasted over four hours, grounding planes around the country as the federal government scrambled to get the standard lines of communications for air traffic controllers back online. Trump’s special interagency group known as the “Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team” will bring together representatives from the FAA, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Defense, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, according to the White House. “As millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday, President Donald J. Trump is making sure the skies stay open and the systems run smoothly,” the White House said in a press release. The FAA reported that 12,462 flights were canceled during the ground stop, which began mid-afternoon on Friday, November 13. The FAA is still investigating the technical hiccup that prompted thousands of planes to be grounded, but a routine router upgrade completed by federal contractor L3Harris Technologies in Arkansas is believed to be at fault. Tiger teams in action The term “tiger team” is sometimes used in corporate settings, but it is more commonly used to describe small, highly-skilled teams convened to solve difficult problems in government and military operations. The most famous tiger team in history is credited with safely guiding NASA’s Apollo 13 mission back to Earth safely, a feat that earned NASA Flight and Mission Operations Director Gene Kranz and his specialized group a Presidential Medal of Freedom. Other U.S. agencies also use tiger teams for specialized problem solving, including the U.S. Department of Labor. The Trump administration appears to have a particular affinity for the term and also stood up a self-described tiger team across the Department of Energy and the Department of the Interior last year to “unleash” the American energy industry. That group later became bogged down wrestling with oil prices and inflation tied to the war in Iran. Beyond being tough to say five times fast, we don’t know a lot about Trump’s transportation tiger team. A White House official told The Daily Wire that the FAA is looking into “near-term” network configuration options and other short term ways to boost the stability of current air traffic control systems while slower modernization efforts move forward. “President Trump and Secretary Duffy have brought together the best and the brightest across the government to ensure what happened last Friday can never happen again,” White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said. “…This team has hit the ground running in modernizing and improving the reliability of the nation’s decades-old air traffic control system.”  Schuster claimed that American skies are already safer thanks to the “tremendous progress” from the tiger team, but reassuring Americans skittish about air safety after a spate of recent scares may not be that easy. Modernizing the U.S. air traffic control system is a major long-term goal shared by multiple presidential administrations and scores of lawmakers, but the ground stop showed that pushing technology fixes in an ancient system that never goes offline poses its own set of risks. Record holiday travel expected In a press release, the U.S. Department of Transportation said it expects to see the “busiest holiday skies in 16 years” with more than 417,000 flights forecast for the nine days beginning on Monday of Thanksgiving week. Tuesday is projected to be the busiest travel day of the period, with more than 52,000 flights scheduled. “From standing up a Tiger Team to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful latest platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we’ve taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations,” U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said. “The American people can rest assured we will be on the clock 24/7 to get families to their destinations safely and on time.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than a week after Nvidia’s board mentioned it would not reinstate Jensen Huang, it renamed him President and CEO. President Trump had intervened with public support for Huang and reportedly even called into a board meeting, urging directors to reconsider their position. While Huang is a visionary leader who has delivered extraordinary results, putting him back at the helm despite an open independent investigation of his conduct may put the company at even greater risk. How will managers hold their teams accountable if the CEO is perceived to be able to violate the company’s code of conduct and lie about it to the board and employees? As an executive and team coach, I’ve seen this situation time and again (albeit not to this extreme), and it creates a near-impossible situation for the rank and file. Leaders must now hold their teams accountable when employees have reason to question that the minimum standards are discretionary. Why people defend problematic high performers Compensation was the most submitted question that then-Interim CEO Colette Kress received during last week’s company-wide meeting. And it makes sense – the stock price dropped sharply when Huang announced his resignation. Yet it’s not just money that likely motivated over 1,600 comments on an internal post, most supporting Huang’s return. There is also a sense of pride in being part of a winning team, one that was synonymous with Huang. In many ways, defending him may feel like defending what they’ve helped build. Moreover, with approximately 60 direct reports, there is no apparent successor – heightening the business risk of replacing him. That, coupled with external political and investor pressure from heavyweights such as Trump, Elon Musk, and Bill Ackman, likely fueled the sentiment that Huang should be reinstated. What happens when exceptions become precedents Employees may trust Huang’s business judgment but question how Nvidia handles misconduct. The implications of the board’s reversal will likely take time to fully materialize. For example, what happens when a less indispensable leader violates company policy or upcoming allegations emerge against Huang or another executive? Will employees become less willing to raise concerns if consequences depend on someone’s perceived value to the company? Huang’s personal missteps may also erode trust and credibility with employees, after reports that he misled company leaders about his affair with Alice Huang have shown he is willing to deceive people in his personal and professional life. Employees may think, what else is he capable of? This may affect employees’ willingness to stake their own reputations behind him. Managers may also struggle to hold people to expectations when employees believe exceptions can be made. One client of mine, whom I’ll call Eliza, is a Chief Revenue Officer with an underperforming VP of Sales who has a long-standing friendship with the CEO. Although the VP of Sales did not perform the basic functions of his role, Eliza couldn’t hold him accountable because the CEO would not back her up. She was responsible for the company’s revenue goal without the authority to deliver it. Ultimately, Eliza gave the CEO an ultimatum – it was either her or her VP. Thankfully theCEO moved him to another department, but the company nearly lost her. Managing a double standard When Jensen returned to the office, an employee shouted, “We love you, Jensen!” And while his return may be welcome to many, it will create a disparity in expectations that managers will have to address. I once worked with a senior executive in a similar situation. Hs team’s frustration with the CEO’s decisions became all-consuming – and he agreed with them. He spent his nights and weekends agonizing, and he found himself adding to their list of grievances in team meetings. He felt awful, and so did his team. I told him he had a decision to make. He could continue with the status quo, or he could acknowledge the reality of the situation and decide whether he wanted to stay or leave the company. He ultimately decided to look for a new job, but in the interim, he focused his team on what they could influence. While he didn’t disclose to his team that he was looking, he did tell them that while they worked for this company, they were responsible for having productive conversations that moved the business forward. If anyone felt they couldn’t do that, he would support them if they decided to leave. This alleviated the burden he felt he was carrying by trying to “protect” his team. Managers who are in the thankless position of serving under a divisive leader are stuck between a rock and a hard place. They are caught between a leader they can’t remove and their employees. Their best bet is to be clear about where their authority begins and ends, and make it clear that their team, including themselves, will be held to a high standard. But the internal cost of doing this when the company’s leader is not held to the same standard is high, and this creates a ripe breeding ground for talented managers and employees to leave. While it is rare for a company to be ensnared in a scandal of this magnitude, leaders often face pressure to overlook the behavior of someone who delivers exceptional results. Overlooking this behavior may seem like the easiest path for continuing to deliver exceptional results–but it comes with a cost: the well-being of the rest of the team. This is why adequate succession planning is so critical, so no one becomes “too major to fail.”.

The industry’s biggest players are joining together to celebrate all the amazing VR games you probably don’t know about (but should).

This year has been difficult for the gaming industry at large, and that’s particularly true for the wonderful niche of VR gaming. Despite some huge setbacks, VR gaming is still alive and well, popping out tons of amazing games this year that you may not have realized. To celebrate those wins, VR studio and publishing label Creature is joined by Future Friends Games to bring back the VR Forever Awards this December.

Throughout the entire festival, you can expect tons of latest game demos on Steam, including over 220 games from nearly 150 developers. While the festival is technically on Steam, Meta Quest still rules the roost in the VR world, so you can expect plenty of surprises for Quest gamers.

It has been revealed that the festival will run from December 3rd to 9th on Steam and will cover the best of VR across six categories: Best Hidden Gem, Best Single Player, Best Multiplayer, Best Ongoing, Most Anticipated Game, and Game of the Year. This year’s judges include Zeena Al-Obaidi (CCO at VR Games Showcase), Ian Hamilton (Founder of Good Virtual Reality), Naysy (Content Creator, VR Forever Ambassador), and Nicholas Sutrich (me!).

In a recent development, the full list of winners and nominees will be announced during the show, but Creature highlights Forefront, Thief VR: Legacy of Shadow, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City, Dungeons of Eternity, Titan Isles, and the ever-popular Hot Dogs, Horseshoes & Hand Grenades 2 as some of the most notable. Visit the VR Forever website to learn more, and check out Naysy’s video above for even more details!

Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

In a recent development, AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today. Whether it's detecting fraudulent transactions, assessing credit risk, forecasting demand, or personalizing customer experiences, organizations are increasingly relying on AI to make faster and smarter decisions.

In a recent development, and naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment. We spend considerable time making sure our models are trained well, our pipelines run efficiently, and our systems can handle production workloads.

But here's something we don't always pay enough attention to: Can we actually trust the data feeding these models?

After all, even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. What's interesting is that these problems don't always show up as technical failures. Sometimes, everything appears to be working perfectly fine.

Imagine a financial institution that has recently deployed an AI-powered loan risk assessment system. The team has spent months preparing the data, training the model, testing its performance, and finally moving it into production.

The deployment goes smoothly. Data pipelines are running on schedule, predictions are being generated, and all the monitoring dashboards are green.

It has been revealed that A few weeks later, however, the business team notices something unusual. The model has started classifying more customers as high risk than expected.

The data science team checks the model configuration. Nothing has changed. The engineering team reviews the pipelines. All jobs have completed successfully. Even the infrastructure looks healthy.

According to recent reports, it turns out that an upstream source system changed the definition of a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income. The field name remained the same, the data type was still numeric, and none of the existing technical validations detected the change.

The pipeline continued running as expected, but the model was now receiving information with a different business meaning.

This brings us to an vital point: Just because an AI pipeline runs successfully doesn't necessarily mean we can trust its output.

Recent findings suggest that building reliable AI systems requires us to look beyond the model itself. We need to understand where the data originates, how it changes as it moves through different systems, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

In this article, we'll explore three important elements of trustworthy AI pipelines (data quality, data lineage, and accountability) and look at how engineering teams can incorporate them into their existing workflows without making the process unnecessarily complicated.

Most modern data pipelines come with some form of operational monitoring. Engineering teams track job completion, execution time, system availability, and processing failures.

These metrics are notable because they help us understand whether our systems are functioning as expected.

Operational monitoring primarily tells us whether a pipeline executed successfully. It doesn't necessarily tell us whether the data being processed is accurate, consistent, or suitable for the model consuming it.

Suppose we're building a loan risk model that uses a customer's debt-to-income ratio as one of its input features.

The calculation is straightforward:.

Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payments / Monthly income.

Now imagine that an upstream system starts supplying annual income instead of monthly income.

In a recent development, the calculation still executes successfully. The values are numeric, the transformation doesn't throw an error, and the model continues generating predictions.

However, the resulting debt-to-income ratio is incorrect because the numerator and denominator represent different time periods.

This is where traditional monitoring falls short.

To build trustworthy AI pipelines, we need to look at different dimensions of system health.

These approaches complement each other.

According to recent reports, A pipeline can be operationally healthy while processing unreliable data. Similarly, a model can continue producing predictions even when the meaning of an key input field has changed.

For engineering teams, the objective should be to identify these problems as early as possible, ideally before they reach downstream models.

We've all heard the phrase "garbage in, garbage out.".

And despite all the progress we've made in artificial intelligence, this principle hasn't changed.

AI models may be capable of processing enormous volumes of data and identifying complex patterns, but they cannot automatically guarantee that the information they're receiving is correct.

This is where data quality becomes key.

Data quality refers to how well information meets the requirements of its intended use. In AI pipelines, it helps us determine whether incoming data is sufficiently reliable for model training, evaluation, or inference.

Let's look at four dimensions that are particularly relevant.

Imagine we're developing a loan risk model that relies on customer income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

What happens if 20% of the incoming records are missing income information?

In a recent development, should we reject those records? Should we replace missing values using an approved statistical method? Or should we flag them for additional review?

There isn't one answer that works for every system.

The right approach depends on the model, the business requirements, and the potential consequences of the decision.

What matters is that missing information is handled deliberately.

For example, replacing missing income with zero may allow the pipeline to continue running, but it could significantly distort the model's predictions.

Validity checks whether values meet expected formats, ranges, and business rules.

Consider a customer record containing the following information:.

The credit utilization value immediately stands out.

Although credit utilization can exceed 100% in certain circumstances, a value of 450% may warrant investigation.

This highlights an important distinction: Not every unusual value is incorrect, and not every technically valid value is meaningful.

A database may accept any numeric value, but the business may need additional rules to determine whether that value is appropriate for the model.

Engineering teams should distinguish between invalid records, unexpected observations, and legitimate exceptions.

This is one of the most common challenges in enterprise data environments.

Imagine two systems providing customer income information.

System A reports annual gross income.

System B reports monthly net income.

Both datasets contain a column called income.

If we combine these datasets without understanding their definitions, we risk introducing inconsistencies into downstream calculations.

According to recent reports, the data may look perfectly fine from a technical perspective. The problem is that the same field represents different business concepts.

This is why data definitions, units, and transformation rules are just as vital as schema validation.

Suppose a model predicts a customer's current financial risk using income information that was last updated 18 months ago.

The data might be accurate, complete, and consistent.

But is it current enough to support the decision?

Different AI applications have different freshness requirements.

A real-time fraud detection model may require near-real-time transaction information, while a long-term forecasting model may work with less frequently updated datasets.

The notable thing is to define these expectations based on how the data will be used.

The good news is that improving data quality doesn't always require sophisticated enterprise tools.

A practical starting point is to define validation rules for the most important input fields.

For example, consider the following conceptual configuration:.

This is an illustrative data quality contract rather than executable configuration for a particular framework.

It defines basic expectations and specifies what should happen when the data fails validation.

Tools such as Great Expectations can help automate these checks. For smaller systems, custom SQL or Python validations may be sufficient.

However, technical validation alone isn't enough.

Remember our original example where the income field changed from gross to net income?

Both values could easily pass a rule requiring income to be greater than zero.

Detecting that kind of glitch requires clear business definitions, communication with upstream systems, and appropriate change management.

In other words, data quality isn't just about checking values. It's also about understanding what those values represent.

Now let's assume our loan risk model generates an unexpectedly high risk score for a customer.

The model output is available, but we want to understand what contributed to the prediction.

We start investigating the input data.

The income information came from a customer application system. Outstanding debt came from another database. Both datasets went through several transformations before reaching the feature engineering pipeline.

The final features were then passed to the model.

At this point, a seemingly simple question becomes surprisingly difficult:.

Where exactly did the information used for this prediction come from?

This is where data lineage becomes valuable.

Data lineage describes how data originates, moves, and changes across different systems.

For AI pipelines, it helps us understand the journey from raw source data to the features used by a model.

A simplified flow might look like this:.

Source Systems → Data Transformation → Feature Engineering → Model Inference → Predictions.

Each stage introduces dependencies that can affect downstream results.

Data lineage can be captured at different levels of detail.

Dataset-level lineage demonstrates relationships between datasets.

Loan Applications → Cleaned Applications → Model Features.

This helps us understand how datasets move through the overall architecture.

However, suppose the model's debt-to-income ratio suddenly changes.

Dataset-level lineage might tell us which datasets were involved, but it may not provide enough detail to identify the affected field.

That's where column-level lineage becomes useful.

debt_to_income_ratio = monthly_debt_payment / monthly_income.

Column-level lineage can show that the resulting feature depends on two upstream attributes.

If one of those attributes changes, engineers can trace the dependency and investigate the impact.

This is especially valuable in environments where multiple reports, applications, and AI models depend on shared data sources.

Large organizations may use dedicated metadata management and lineage platforms.

However, smaller teams can start by capturing essential metadata during pipeline execution.

OpenLineage provides an open standard for collecting and exchanging lineage metadata across supported systems.

For more detailed prediction-level investigations, teams may also need to retain feature snapshots or inference logs, subject to privacy and retention requirements.

It's important to understand that lineage doesn't automatically guarantee data accuracy.

A pipeline can be perfectly documented and still contain incorrect transformation logic.

But when something goes wrong, lineage gives engineering teams a clearer starting point for investigation.

Instead of searching across multiple systems and trying to reconstruct dependencies manually, they can identify where data originated and how it changed along the way.

Let's consider another situation.

An AI model starts producing unexpected results.

The data science team checks the model and finds no issues.

The data engineering team confirms that the pipelines are running successfully.

The source-system team verifies that data was delivered according to its interface.

Yet the problem remains unresolved.

Everyone has completed their individual checks, but nobody has identified who should coordinate the investigation.

This is where accountability becomes important.

In a recent development, AI pipelines often involve multiple teams responsible for different stages of the data lifecycle. Without clearly defined ownership, even relatively simple concerns can take longer to resolve.

A practical accountability framework should distinguish between three responsibilities.

Data owners are responsible for defining the business meaning and expected quality of critical information.

For example, someone needs to determine whether an income field represents gross income, net income, or another financial measure.

These definitions should be documented and communicated to downstream consumers.

Data engineering and platform teams typically manage data ingestion, transformations, validation mechanisms, and pipeline operations.

Their responsibilities may include implementing quality checks, monitoring failures, and assessing the technical impact of changes.

However, technical teams shouldn't be expected to make business-definition decisions without appropriate input.

Data science and ML engineering teams are responsible for evaluating model behavior, managing model versions, and assessing how changes in input data may affect predictions.

If a critical feature changes, the model team may need to determine whether additional testing, recalibration, or retraining is required.

Defining ownership is useful, but connecting it to an operational process is even more key.

Consider a critical data quality failure during feature generation.

A response process might look like this:.

The exact workflow will vary depending on the organization and the risk associated with the application.

The objective is to ensure that technical alerts lead to clear actions.

After all, an alert that nobody owns is just another notification waiting to be ignored.

So far, we've discussed why data quality, lineage, and accountability matter.

But how can we bring these concepts into everyday engineering practices?

Here are five controls that teams can introduce without redesigning their entire architecture.

Data contracts define expectations between data producers and consumers.

They can document schemas, field definitions, units, freshness requirements, and compatibility expectations.

For example, rather than specifying only that annual_income is numeric, a contract should clarify whether it represents gross or net income, the currency, and the applicable time period.

This reduces the risk of downstream systems misinterpreting technically valid information.

Quality gates validate critical data before it progresses through the pipeline.

These checks can be implemented during ingestion, transformation, feature generation, or inference.

For example, a feature engineering process calculating debt-to-income ratios should verify that debt and income values use compatible time periods.

Recent findings suggest that failure handling should reflect the severity of the issue. Some records may be quarantined, while more serious failures may require stopping the pipeline.

Pipeline execution should produce sufficient metadata to identify source datasets, transformations, and downstream outputs.

Where appropriate, teams should also capture model and feature versions associated with predictions.

This information supports impact analysis, debugging, and investigation when unexpected results occur.

AI systems evolve continuously.

Datasets change, transformation logic is updated, features are modified, and models are retrained.

Versioning helps engineering teams understand which components were active at a particular point in time.

Relevant evidence may include pipeline configurations, dataset snapshots, model versions, validation outcomes, and deployment records.

Retention should be designed around operational requirements, privacy considerations, and applicable policies rather than storing everything indefinitely.

Every critical data element or pipeline component should have an identified owner or responsible team.

More importantly, ownership should connect directly to incident management and change approval processes.

If a source definition changes, teams should know who evaluates the impact.

If a quality gate fails, the responsible team should receive the alert.

If model performance deteriorates, the investigation should have a clear escalation path.

These controls are most effective when they become part of normal development and deployment practices rather than separate administrative activities.

Implementing comprehensive governance across an entire data environment can be challenging, particularly for organizations with legacy systems and complex dependencies.

A more effective approach is to begin with one critical AI pipeline.

For example, a team operating a loan risk model could start by identifying the inputs that have the greatest influence on its predictions.

These might include income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

For each critical input, the team can document five things:.

Once these foundations are established, the team can implement automated checks and gradually extend the approach to additional datasets.

This incremental strategy also makes it easier to demonstrate the value of governance controls.

For instance, teams can track how quickly data-related incidents are detected, how long investigations take, and whether recurring issues are reduced.

The goal isn't to introduce governance for its own sake.

It's to improve the reliability, maintainability, and transparency of the systems developers are responsible for operating.

Explainable AI has become an important topic in machine learning.

Techniques such as feature importance analysis and SHAP can help teams understand which inputs influence model predictions.

However, explainability and data trustworthiness address different problems.

Suppose a model explanation identifies debt-to-income ratio as a major contributor to a customer's high-risk classification.

That explanation may accurately describe the model's behavior.

But if the debt-to-income ratio was calculated using an incorrectly defined income field, the explanation alone may not reveal the underlying data problem.

This highlights the importance of evaluating AI systems across multiple dimensions.

Model explainability helps us understand how predictions are generated.

Data quality helps establish whether inputs satisfy defined expectations.

Data lineage provides visibility into where information originated and how it was transformed.

Accountability ensures that identified problems can be investigated and addressed.

These capabilities are complementary rather than interchangeable.

According to recent reports, none independently guarantees that an AI system is accurate, fair, secure, or compliant. Together, however, they provide a stronger foundation for evaluating and improving system reliability.

As AI systems become more integrated into business processes, engineering teams face increasing expectations around reliability, transparency, and accountability.

Model accuracy and operational performance remain essential, but they represent only part of the overall picture.

A pipeline can execute successfully while processing inconsistent information. A model can generate predictions using features whose definitions have changed. And an explanation can describe a model's behavior without identifying problems in the underlying data.

Building trustworthy AI therefore requires attention to the entire data lifecycle.

Data quality controls help detect unreliable inputs. Lineage provides visibility into how information moves through systems. Clear ownership ensures that issues can be investigated and resolved.

Importantly, these practices don't need to begin with large-scale governance programs or expensive technology investments.

Engineering teams can start with a single critical pipeline, identify its most key data elements, establish quality expectations, and introduce basic traceability and accountability mechanisms.

Over time, these practices can become part of standard development and deployment workflows.

It has been revealed that the real measure of a trustworthy AI pipeline isn't simply whether it produces a prediction. It's whether the organization can understand, validate, and take responsibility for the information behind that prediction.

After all, a green dashboard is reassuring. But it shouldn't be the only evidence that an AI system is working as intended.

Set to launch on December 8, Nothing has confirmed its mysterious AI product will be called “Ear (note),” and it’s an AI recorder with earbuds inside.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Nothing has confirmed that its upcoming AI product is “Ear (note).” This builds on a pair of earbuds by turning the charging case into an AI-powered recorder.

The case has a “Talk” button, like Ear (3), which can be used to record your own voice, where a record button enables the ability to “record and transcribe conversations.” Ear (3a)’s ability to record audio from the earbuds will also carry over to Ear (note), giving the product the ability to record both conversations in person and over the phone.

Nothing is entering a crowded market here with products from Plaud, Amazon, and countless others already offering AI recording/transcribing products, but building in earbuds is indeed a unique selling point.

It has been revealed that nothing Ear (note) is launching on December 8, though pricing is unclear. Pei’s comments suggest a subscription will be used in some capacity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool changers — 3D printers with multiple heads — have been a major focus of the industry for more than a year, and for good reason. Multiple heads mean you don’t have to purge the nozzle every time your print swaps colors or materials, which has the dual benefit of making complex prints much faster while saving a massive amount of filament waste or “poop,” which is a problem with more traditional multi-color AMS, single-toolhead printers.

Industry observers note that but while these tool changers typically cost multiple thousands of dollars a few years ago, they’ve gotten much more affordable in the past year, starting with Snapmaker’s sub-$1,000 U1 (now just $699) and then Fashforge’s Creator 5 not long after. And both of those printers, plus a traditional four-color AMS printer designed to minimize wasted filament, are all on sale at their lowest-ever prices as we head into Black Friday.So if you’re thinking of diving into the 3D printing realm or your existing printer is getting long in the tooth, now is a great time to make the leap to a tool changer and see how it can change your printing game — or perhaps your printing business.

In a recent development, snapmaker’s U1 kicked off the affordable tool changer craze around this time last year, with an early Kickstarter price of $799 and a full retail price of $999. But now it’s widely available and on sale for $100 less than ever. When we reviewed the U1, we praised its roomy build area (270 mm cubed), direct-drive tool heads, and its four-head tool-changing capabilities, earning it 4.5 stars and a spot on our best 3D printers list.

Last year, this tool-changer was the most anticipated upcoming printer around. With four heads for swapping colors or materials without the need to "poop," it can breeze through complex multicolor prints much faster than single-head printers, without wasting nearly as much filament.

On the heels of the U1, Flashforge released the Creator 5, a tool changer that’s a bit more basic, but still a solid machine (we gave it 4 stars in our review), priced even lower than the Snapmaker, both when it debuted (at $699) and now, when it’s on sale for $100 less. You can grab that base model, or the Creator 5 Pro, which adds an enclosure with a cooling fan and filtration for more consistent temperatures, which can prevent warping and generally lead to better prints.

This open CoreXY 3D printer has four toolheads, is rated for head swaps that take 7 seconds, and sports a 256 mm X3 build volume.

In a recent development, an upgraded version of the Creator 5, you get the same 4 tool heads and build volume, now with an enclosed chamber with a fan and filter. If you're sensitive to PLA or PETG fumes, your workspace lacks ventilation (or is drafty), or you print with more exotic filaments, it's worth paying extra for.

Last up, and least expensive on this list, is Anycubic’s Kobra X. This isn’t a tool changer, as it has a single head. Instead, it’s a more traditional four-color printer that aims to reduce filament waste by putting the filament cutter much closer to the nozzle tip. It also takes up less space, as it's designed to keep four filament spools on a rack up top rather than a separate AMD.I’ve owned this printer for going on a year, and you’ll still see a lot of filament waste when tackling multi-color prints, but it does create less poop than previous printers I’ve owned. And if you can’t afford to spend more than $500, the Kobra X delivers solid multi-color printing at a price that’s tough to beat. It’s right now on sale for its lowest-ever price of just $279.

Industry observers note that this low-priced, space-saving four-color 3D printer has a 260 mm X3 build volume, houses four filament spools up top, and is quick when swapping filaments. It also saves filament waste by cutting closer to the nozzle tip when switching, but it will still "poop," and can waste a lot of filament if you regularly tackle multi-color prints.
